newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Toyota deal signals growth for NZ boat builders.
newsitem.headline: Toyota deal signals growth for NZ boat builders.

text.p: Japan's largest carmaker has given two small companies the chance to put New Zealand's boat-building industry on the international map.
McDell Marine Ltd along with Circa Engineering and Marine Ltd have secured contracts to build Toyota's first-ever motorboat.
If all goes well, the companies say the deal could lead to significant industry growth.
"It's a major coup for New Zealand's boat-building industry," said Logan Cripps, director at Circa, which builds aluminium hulls and fits them with Toyota engines.
McDell, fibre-glass specialists, fit out the hulls and assembles the boat "to the point where you can turn the key and drive it away", managing director Kim McDell said.
TOYOTA MOTORBOATS FOR EXPORT
Toyota Japan announced its first foray into the marine business on December 18, saying it planned to develop a range of boats of varying sizes and a full line-up of marine engines.
The first production run last year of 15 highly specified 8.5 metre (28 foot) cabin-cruisers developed for export to Japan is only the first of a range of powerboats being considered.

"Initially, the multi-million dollar export deal is for one year only, but this can be extended and the range of boats expanded if the boats sell well in Japan," said Toyota New Zealand managing director Bob Field.
There are no plans to sell the boats in New Zealand.
Two have already been completed and shipped to Japan, where they will be displayed at boat shows early this year before going on sale there.
Toyota has not disclosed how much the boats will cost, but industry experts said the cabin-cruisers would sell for between 15 million yen (US$131,000) and 20 million yen in Japan.
A Toyota Japan spokesman said the company was targeting annual boat and marine engine sales of about 50 billion yen by early next century.
AMERICA'S CUP WIN HIGHLIGHTS BOAT-BUILDING EXPERTISE
Toyota spent 18 months looking for the right companies to build its first boat.
And New Zealand's triumph in lifting yachting's prized America's Cup from the United States in 1995 played a major role in New Zealand boat builders clinching the Toyota deal.
"Our America's Cup win made a deep impression in Japan about New Zealand's ability to build boats," Field said.
He said Toyota was linked as a sponsor to Team New Zealand, the syndicate that beat the San Diego Yacht Club team lead by Dennis Conner to bring the "Auld Mug" down under.
The next America's Cup regatta is to be held off Auckland in 2000 and the financial benefits for the country have been estimated to be in excess of NZ$2 billion.
But Field said the spinoffs in terms of attracting other business revenue were incalculable.

"The benefit of winning that America's Cup -- because it's a technology contest as much as a sporting contest -- I don't think anyone's really put a proper value on it," he said. "It's hugely important and in this case was absolutely critical."
Circa and McDell agree that the win gave New Zealand huge kudos in terms of technology, but say it also drew attention to New Zealanders' natural affinity with the ocean.
HUGE POTENTIAL FOR BOAT BUILDERS

The Toyota project has given McDell and Circa the chance to prove their international competitiveness. If they succeed, both say the potential for growth in the New Zealand boat building industry as a whole is significant.

"McDell and Circa have got to perform. But if they do perform, if we can maintain all the boat production in New Zealand, then it has the potential to be the biggest marine export operation in the country," Field said.
Kim McDell said if New Zealand was able to retain the Toyota business, it could attract other large clients to its shores.
"The key factor at the end of the day is that we can be internationally competitive -- that's the key issue. If that can be proved, I'm sure other business will flow." (US$1 = NZ$1.41)
